target: AG1's claim that a national Election Day holiday would directly remove time barriers and make it far easier for more eligible people to vote.
objection: A federal holiday does not automatically give most workers paid time off. Private employers generally are not required to close or pay employees for federal holidays, especially in retail and service jobs, so low-income workers may still have to work and the scheduling barrier would remain for the people most constrained by time.

target: AG2's claim that a national holiday would not reliably remove the time barrier because many workers would still have to work.
objection: For many employees, federal holidays are treated as days when workplaces close or grant time off, so the claim that a holiday does not generally translate into paid time off is too strong. A national holiday would still reduce scheduling conflicts for a substantial portion of the population.

target: AG1's reliance on the idea that a holiday meaningfully reduces scheduling conflicts for most voters.
objection: Because private employers are not required to close or provide paid leave on a federal holiday, many workers in retail and service jobs would still be scheduled to work. That means the holiday does not reliably reduce the time barrier for the people most likely to be constrained by it.

target: AG2's argument that a holiday will not reliably reduce the time barrier because employers may still schedule workers.
objection: National-holiday timing has worked in other democracies, and the barrier is not only employer-paid leave. A holiday shifts the broader school/work/calendar context, making voting more feasible for many people even if some essential workers remain scheduled.

target: AG1's assumption that a holiday broadly provides usable time to vote.
objection: The federal-holiday designation does not guarantee real, takeable time for the majority of workers, especially low-income shift workers, because employers are not required to close or pay them to be off. So the holiday does not reliably remove the scheduling barrier for the workers who most need it.

target: AG2's assumption that only explicit employer-paid leave can solve the time barrier.
objection: A national holiday could be implemented as paid time off or with a direct time-off requirement that protects wages, which would allow workers in shift-based jobs to vote without losing income. With those protections, the holiday would in fact remove the main schedule conflict.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday creates paid, protected time for workers.
objection: Making Election Day a national holiday does not itself provide paid, wage-protected time. Without a separate leave mandate, many retail and service workers would still be scheduled to work, so the holiday is not a dependable way to remove the barrier.

target: AG2's assumption that the time barrier is only about employer-provided paid leave.
objection: For many voters, especially parents and caregivers, the major conflict is between Election Day and school or childcare schedules. A national holiday would close schools and ease caregiving routines, reducing scheduling friction even if some employers remain open.

target: AG2's broader claim that a holiday is ineffective because it does not guarantee paid leave from every employer.
objection: The argument is too narrow because it treats time to vote as depending only on employer-paid leave. A national holiday changes the practical calendar and civic rhythm, reducing routine friction and making voting easier to fit into daily life for many people.

target: AG1's overall claim that Election Day should be a holiday because it reduces scheduling barriers and increases turnout.
objection: Research indicates that simply designating Election Day as a holiday does not meaningfully increase turnout compared with other reforms, so the policy is a low-impact and unreliable way to improve participation. More targeted measures like voting time-off laws and automatic voter registration are more effective.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday will not reach low-income workers or meaningfully improve turnout.
objection: Low-income households are often constrained by school, childcare, and work schedules, so moving Election Day to a broadly recognized non-working civic day reduces the very frictions they face. The holiday also has broad public support and international precedent, showing it is a practical access reform.

target: AG1's assumption that a federal holiday will give most voters usable daytime availability, especially low-income workers.
objection: A federal holiday does not automatically create usable, non-working time because private employers are not required to close or pay workers. Low-income workers in retail, service, and shift jobs are often still scheduled to work, so the holiday's symbolic change does not reliably translate into actual time to vote.

target: AG2's claim that low-income workers will not reliably benefit from a holiday.
objection: Low-income voters are often constrained by rigid school, childcare, and work schedules, so a national holiday still lowers the practical hurdle for many of them. It changes the calendar in a way that makes voting easier to plan around, even if some employers remain open.

target: AG1's claim that low-income voters will benefit because a holiday reduces scheduling friction even without enforceable paid time off.
objection: For low-income voters, the binding constraint is often the inability to absorb lost wages. Since a federal holiday does not force private employers to close or pay time off, many workers still have to choose between working and voting, so the holiday mainly helps people who already have flexibility.

target: AG2's contention that low-income workers will not benefit because the holiday lacks guaranteed paid or enforceable time.
objection: The main barrier is not lack of civic interest but the mismatch between voting and ordinary work, school, and caregiving schedules. A national holiday changes those routines and still reduces the hurdle for many low-income households, even if it does not guarantee paid leave from every employer.

target: AG1's assumption that a federal holiday substantially changes the day-to-day calendar for low-income workers.
objection: A federal holiday does not require employers to close or provide paid time off, so many retail, service, and shift workers will still be scheduled. That means the holiday does not reliably create the paid, protected daytime availability needed to make voting easy for low-income workers.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday will not reliably create workable daytime availability for low-income voters.
objection: Election Day as a national holiday would align schools and many workplaces with the federal calendar and make it easier for households to plan voting around normal daytime availability. That reduces the scheduling friction that often prevents low-income voters from participating.

target: AG1's assumption that a national holiday meaningfully converts Election Day into usable, paid daytime availability for low-income voters.
objection: A federal holiday does not mandate employer closure or paid leave, so many low-income workers in shift jobs still face the same wage-loss or job-risk tradeoff. The claimed reduction in scheduling barriers is therefore not dependable without direct time-off protections.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday will not meaningfully increase turnout or help low-income voters.
objection: The main barrier for many eligible Americans is lack of workable time, not lack of interest. A widely observed national holiday changes school, work, and caregiving routines, making it easier to vote during normal daytime hours and reducing the friction that leads people to miss voting.
